answer: Use the read-only spectrum-monitoring command: show spectrum-monitoring-<name>/<direction>/<center-frequency> [width] [lower-frequency] [upper-frequency] [target-actual-power] [power-actual] [psd-actual]. direction is ingress or egress, default egress, and only egress is currently supported; center-frequency is the band slice center frequency in MHz, managed by the system. width is the received NMC width in MHz, default 50000. power-actual is the currently received power in dBm, default -99, where -99 means the power has not yet been measured by the OCM at the DGE2 card or no power was detected; on egress it is calibrated at the DWDM line port output. target-actual-power (default -99dBm) is the ATPS-calculated target, relevant only when target-power-setting = auto. psd-actual is the calculated Power Spectral Density in nW/GHz to 2-digit precision, default not-applicable, and does not depend on spectral width. Example: show spectrum-monitoring-1-7-dwdm-line2/egress/191968750.

Read the contention-check-status attribute on the super-channel. It is settable on add (add super-channel-<name> carriers <value> carrier-mode <value> [label] [admin-state] [alarm-report-control] [contention-check-status]) and readable with show super-channel-<name> contention-check-status. Values are pending, success, overridden and failk, with pending as the default. The status is the Contention Check state set via DNA in openwave mode, and it is only applicable if openwave-contention-check is enabled at the super-channel-group level. openwave-contention-check enables the DNA-assisted contention control mechanism in openwave mode; its values are false and true, default false, and it is configured with add/set super-channel-group-<name> openwave-contention-check <value>. The related line-system-mode attribute defaults to openwave. Both commands run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

-m is the merge flag: Merge configuration, meaning the command will not fail if the entity already exists. The guide states the add command for super-channel-group works in merge mode only, so the -m flag performs a best-effort add: if the target entity does not exist it is created, and if it already exists it is updated with whatever attributes are present on the add command. Full syntax: add -m super-channel-group-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <lock|unlock|maintenance>] [auto-in-service-enabled <value>] [valid-signal-time <value>] [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>] [line-system-mode <value>] [openwave-contention-check <value>]. Defaults for those attributes are admin-state unlock, alarm-report-control allowed, auto-in-service-enabled false, line-system-mode openwave, and valid-signal-time 480 minutes (range 1..7200). The same -m merge flag is documented for comm-channel.

Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. carrier-mode is an acronymized handle of the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, string length 1...15, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, for example 600E.84P, 100X.73U or 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier in gbps, which is the per-mode capacity you are after. client-mode is the digital client mode mapped into and transported by the carriers in the superchannel, either ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate, application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for (string 1...15), compatibility-id identifies carrier modes applicable simultaneously, status is the state of the carrier mode, and supported-subtypes lists supported subtypes (string 0..32, maximum 20 elements).

Query the supported-gain-range object: show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. gain-range-type selects which of the three ranges you want and takes the values low, high or standard. gain-range-min returns the minimum settable gain-target for that type of range and gain-range-max returns the maximum settable gain-target, both of type gain-value; neither has a documented default (n/a), because the numbers are reported per instance rather than fixed by the guide. All parameters are used in show only; there is no set form. The name key is described in the parameter table as a flag to enable or disable access control, with values true/false and default false.

Different power profiles are supported to reflect different scenarios when using a card. The user can define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a given card type offers, use show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. card-type is the card type (string) and name is the profile name (string). profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0...255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, type decimal64. default is true or false and tells you whether that profile is the default one. All fields are show only; the command reports capability, it does not assign the profile.

The router ID comes from the router-id-mode attribute on the bgp-instance. router-id-mode takes use-loopback or manual and defaults to use-loopback, meaning the instance takes the loopback IP as its router ID unless you switch it to manual. When you need an explicit value, set the router-id attribute, which accepts an IPv6 or IPv4 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6, and it has no default. Syntax: add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], with set and delete forms available; instance-id is a string of length 1...255 and local-as is a number in the range 1..4294967295. The command runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example from the guide: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback.

On bgp-neighbor the three timers are connect-retry-interval, hold-time and keepalive-interval. connect-retry-interval is the seconds between attempts to establish a session with the peer, range 1..65535, default 120. hold-time is the seconds a session is considered active with no keepalive or other messages from the peer, range 3..65535, default 90, and is typically set to 3x the keepalive-interval. keepalive-interval is the seconds between keepalive transmissions, range 1..21845, default 30, typically 1/3 of the hold-time. The negotiated value is read back with negotiated-hold-time (0..65535, default 0). Yes, you can authenticate: secure-session sets the authentication method of the session to the peer and takes none or TCP-MD5, defaulting to none, with password supplying the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII, string 0..80. All are set via add/set bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address>.

The routes to be advertised to an external AS must already exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole, for example on add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> special-next-hop blackhole (the same parameter exists on ipv6-static-route). Beyond that, the bgp-network object itself just names what is exported: add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>, where instance-id is a string 1...255, remote-address is the peer in IPv4 or IPv6 form (0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported) and network-prefix is a decimal 1..64 or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured.

The mtu attribute of comm-channel is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when the mode is L3. The range is platform-dependent: 1280..1500 octets on the 1830 GX G30, and 1280..9202 octets on the 1830 GX G40. It is a uint16 integer. The default is 1500; on the 1830 GX G40 the per-interface-type defaults are 1518 for DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4. Set it with add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [mtu <value>] or set comm-channel-<name> mtu <value>, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The matching receive parameter, mru, is an integer in the range 64..1500 octets with default 1500 and is likewise only available in L3 mode.

LLDP is off by default: lldp-admin-status on comm-eth defaults to disabled, and its values are tx-only (transmits frames but does not store remote system information), rx-only (receives but does not transmit), tx-and-rx, and disabled. It cannot be modified if the mode is L1. Enable it with, for example, set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds, default 30. lldp-mgmt-addr-if picks which interface IP is advertised as the management address (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only), L0-MGMT); it must be set explicitly and applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled; rate (1/10/100/1000/10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum), duplex-mode (default full) and flow-control (default disabled) are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled.

Use the global dhcp-relay command: set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>], readable with show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]. It runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with disabled as the default, so relay is off until you pick an address family. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6, with no default; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples from the guide: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, and set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3. Per-interface activation is separate: if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled must also be set true on each interface, and it obeys these global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. Its values are manual, dhcp and both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts name servers from DHCP as well as ones you configure. Syntax: set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is the flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. search is the DNS-search-suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Per-server origin is tracked separately on dns-server, whose origin attribute is dhcp or manual with default manual.

Add a name server with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server; delete dns-server-<address> removes it and show dns-server-<address> [origin] displays it, all in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The origin attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where an entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the address has been manually configured. The default is manual. origin is also writable, so the user can convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one just by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. Example from the guide: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. The system-wide equivalent is the dns assignment-method attribute (manual, dhcp, both; default both).

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is per interface: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>] and show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. It is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on this interface; it takes true or false and defaults to false, and it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global set dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (not the default disabled) with a server-address configured for the interface setting to have effect. Examples from the guide: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true, and show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled. The interface object also lists an if-dhcp-relay attribute (false/true, default false) deciding on which interface the DHCP/v6 relay can run.

By default it is static and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> ..., ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive packets on each. protection-mode is the user-given protection mode, with values unknown (transient, output only), protected (protected by redundant ports) and unprotected (no port redundancy); it defaults to protected. The read-only protection-state reports the current protection with the same value set and defaults to unknown. Other defaults on add: admin-state unlock (lock, unlock, maintenance), alarm-report-control allowed, proxy-arp-enabled false (applicable only to the DCN interface). Note that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface.

Yes, that is exactly what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings a destination and its result takes action on configured static routes. Create one with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action taken when monitoring goes into failed state; its values are none and withdraw, and the default is withdraw. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the instance is not active until it is configured. probe-interval is 0...60 seconds, default 5; drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1; enabled defaults to true. The route side reports monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>. Read it back with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. The command runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and there is a pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. if-name is the interface object identifier, string length 0..64; type ? after ipv4-address- to list the available interfaces. Certain addresses are disallowed: those beginning with 0 (current network), those beginning with 127 (loopback), and those beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). netmask is the subnet expressed as a netmask and only valid netmasks are accepted. origin is show-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0.

distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. Syntax: add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. For a discard route, use special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole). Blackhole static routes exist because routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. advertised (true/false, default false) advertises the route in the routing protocol, as an AS external route for OSPF if OSPF is an ASBR; origin is manual or dhcp, default manual. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165.

It is the same shape but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported only on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. if-name is the interface object identifier, string length 0..64; type ? after ipv6-address- to see the object completion options. origin is show-only with values static, dhcp and auto-config, default static. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64.

Yes. The guide notes that static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and name DCN-B on the interface parameter, for example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B. The VRF bound to the interface must match the VRF provided on the static route. Defaults are distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), and special-next-hop blackhole for discard routes. The command is available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. The equivalent primary-interface form is add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. There may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to the LLDP neighbor and direction is ingress or egress. address is the string identifying the management address component of the remote system, length 0..64, whose purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype is unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the integer interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote agent, string 0..128.

They report the same kind of data from opposite ends, and differ in their key. management-address is keyed with a direction: show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>, where direction is ingress or egress. management-address-local drops that key: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>, and show management-address-local displays the management address information from the local LLDP ports. Both take the same optional fields if-subtype, if-id and address-oid, and both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. if-subtype is unknown (interface is not known), if-index (identifier based on the ifIndex MIB object) or system-port-number (identifier based on the system port numbering convention). address is a string 0..64 used to contact the management entity and address-oid is a string 0..128; on management-address-local the guide notes that address-oid is currently an empty string.

Yes, it is the use-as-source attribute of the networking object. Syntax: set networking [use-as-source <value>] and show networking [use-as-source], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. use-as-source is described as the interface to use as source address; its value is a string of length 0..64 and it has no default (n/a). You give it an interface name rather than a literal address. Example from the guide: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking displays the current setting. use-as-source is the only parameter the networking command defines.

show networking-services. That is the whole syntax: the command is used to show the list of network services, it takes no parameters, and it is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. There is no set form, only show. The guide's example is simply show networking-services. The related networking command is separate and carries the single use-as-source attribute (set networking use-as-source <interface>).
